mcqs.question: Which of the following expressions correctly defines the angular momentum \(\mathbf{L}\) of a particle of mass \(m\) moving with linear momentum \(\mathbf{p}\) at a position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) from the origin?
mcqs.explanation: Angular momentum of a particle is defined as the vector cross product of its position vector \(\mathbf{r}\) and linear momentum \(\mathbf{p}\): \(\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{p}\). Option B states this definition. Option A adds vectors, which is incorrect; Option C is a dot product; Option D includes an unnecessary factor of 1/2.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate torque to rate of change of angular momentum
mcqs.question: A uniform disc is initially at rest on a frictionless axle. A constant torque of \(5\,\text{N·m}\) is applied about its central axis. Which equation correctly relates the applied torque to the disc's angular momentum after a time \(t\)?
mcqs.explanation: Torque is the time derivative of angular momentum: \(\tau = d\mathbf{L}/dt\). This fundamental relation holds for any rigid body. Option A expresses this correctly. Options B, C, and D misuse the relationship and are incorrect.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements reflects a common misconception about the conservation of angular momentum?

options.A: If no external torque acts on a system, its total angular momentum remains constant.
options.B: Angular momentum can change even when the net external torque is zero.
options.C: The vector nature of angular momentum must be considered when applying conservation.
options.D: Conservation of angular momentum is analogous to conservation of linear momentum.

mcqs.answer: Angular momentum can change even when the net external torque is zero.
mcqs.explanation: Statement B is a misconception; in the absence of external torque, angular momentum is conserved and cannot change. Statements A, C, and D are correct descriptions of the conservation principle.

mcqs.learning_point: Apply angular-momentum conservation to simple systems
mcqs.question: A figure skater spins with her arms extended. Her moment of inertia is \(5\,\text{kg·m}^2\) and her angular speed is \(2\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\). She then pulls her arms in, reducing her moment of inertia to \(2\,\text{kg·m}^2\). Assuming no external torque, what is her new angular speed?
mcqs.explanation: Conservation of angular momentum gives \(I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2\). Substituting: \(5\times2 = 2\times\omega_2\) → \(\omega_2 = 10/2 = 5\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\). Option C is correct. Options A, B, and D result from incorrect algebra.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes angular momentum from linear momentum?

options.A: Both are scalar quantities; angular momentum depends on the choice of origin, while linear momentum does not.
options.B: Linear momentum is a vector defined as \(m\mathbf{v}\); angular momentum is a vector defined as \(\mathbf{r}\times m\mathbf{v}\) and depends on the reference point.
options.C: Angular momentum is always larger in magnitude than linear momentum for the same mass and speed.
options.D: Linear momentum is conserved only in rotational motion, whereas angular momentum is conserved only in translational motion.

mcqs.answer: Linear momentum is a vector defined as \(m\mathbf{v}\); angular momentum is a vector defined as \(\mathbf{r}\times m\mathbf{v}\) and depends on the reference point.
mcqs.explanation: Option B correctly states that linear momentum is \(\mathbf{p}=m\mathbf{v}\) and angular momentum is \(\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{p}\), with \(\mathbf{L}\) depending on the chosen origin. Option A incorrectly calls them scalars. Option C is not generally true. Option D reverses the contexts of conservation.

mcqs.learning_point: Relate torque to rate of change of angular momentum
mcqs.question: A rigid body initially has angular momentum \(\mathbf{L}_0\). A constant external torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) acts on it for a time \(t\). Which expression gives the angular momentum \(\mathbf{L}\) after this interval?
mcqs.explanation: From \(\boldsymbol{\tau}=d\mathbf{L}/dt\), integrating over time gives \(\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{L}_0+\boldsymbol{\tau}t\) for constant torque. Option B reflects this. Option A has the wrong sign, Option C omits the initial angular momentum, and Option D is mathematically unrelated.

mcqs.question: The angular momentum of an isolated system remains constant provided that:

options.A: The net external force on the system is zero.
options.B: The net external torque on the system is zero.
options.C: The system's mass does not change.
options.D: The system moves at a constant linear speed.

mcqs.answer: The net external torque on the system is zero.
mcqs.explanation: Conservation of angular momentum requires that the resultant external torque acting on the system be zero. Force alone (Option A) does not guarantee torque conservation. Options C and D are unrelated to angular momentum conservation.

mcqs.learning_point: Apply angular-momentum conservation to simple systems
mcqs.question: When a spinning ice skater pulls her arms inward, what happens to her angular speed and why?

options.A: Angular speed decreases because the skater’s mass increases.
options.B: Angular speed remains unchanged because angular momentum is not conserved in human motion.
options.C: Angular speed increases because her moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum stays constant.
options.D: Angular speed increases because an external torque is applied by the skater’s muscles.

mcqs.answer: Angular speed increases because her moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum stays constant.
mcqs.explanation: With no external torque, angular momentum is conserved. Pulling the arms in reduces the moment of inertia; to keep \(I\omega\) constant, \(\omega\) must increase. Option C captures this. Option A incorrectly links mass to speed; Option B denies conservation; Option D incorrectly attributes the change to an external torque.
